Hi all — I think SimpleGraph may be missing a small metric-ball API, and I wanted to sanity-check the design before opening a PR.

I’m proposing a definition based on edist, so disconnected vertices stay at distance ⊤ and are excluded from finite-radius balls. The draft is roughly:

def SimpleGraph.closedBall (G : SimpleGraph V) (c : V) (r : ℕ∞) : Set V :=
{v | G.edist c v ≤ r}

with a small first-pass API:

  • membership lemma
  • radius 0 / ⊤
  • center membership
  • monotonicity in radius
  • symmetry membership lemma

Does this look like the right definition / name / file for upstream? I was planning to add it to Combinatorics.SimpleGraph.Metric`.

Small follow-up: after posting this, I noticed the recent discussion here about the SimpleGraph/digraph refactor work.

Does that change the advice on whether a small SimpleGraph metric-ball API is worth upstreaming right now? My draft is intentionally narrow (edist-based closed balls plus a few basic lemmas), but if this should wait or be phrased against a more general abstraction, I’d rather know before polishing a PR.

I was thinking this should be added indeed so thank you :) notably I wanted a bound on the size of a ball in terms of the maximal degree. I don't see any reason to wait until the refactor as we will have to bring a lot of things anyway.

Metrics have 4 types of balls: docs#Metric.ball, docs#Metric.eball, docs#Metric.closedBall, docs#Metric.closedEBall. You defined a closedEBall without the E.
I think that for graphs (and ℕ∞-valued metrics in general), open eballs are more useful: for n : ℕ we have closedEBall v n = eball v (n + 1), and closedEBall v ⊤ = .univ, but with open eballs we get eball v ⊤ = (G.connectedComponentMk v).supp which seems more useful.
What about defining a docs#PseudoEMetricSpace instead? Then we get all the balls for free from the Metric API

Thank you Laura & Snir, this is very helpful.

Snir, that makes sense. I was indeed defining the closed edist ball, not the open one, and your point about eball v ⊤ giving the connected-component support is especially convincing.

The PseudoEMetricSpace suggestion also seems like the more upstream-shaped approach if it fits cleanly.

Would you recommend I explore that first, and only fall back to graph-specific defs/lemmas if the instance route turns out to be awkward? I’m happy to narrow the scope to whatever is most natural for mathlib.
Yes, but I don't think it can be an instance since it requires choosing a specific graph, it'll have to be a def.

Oh, btw, I was thinking one special thing about balls on graphs is that there is a notion of child and parent there. I don't know if you want to implement it there or it should be done more generally for rooted graphs (or has been done).

Thanks y'all! This is really helpful.

Snir, that makes sense: not an instance on V, but a graph-parameterized def like G.toPseudoEMetricSpace and then reuse the existing metric API from there. Laura, the rooted/parent-child point also seems very natural, but probably as a follow-up once the basic metric layer is in place.

I’ll keep the scope narrow and explore the toPseudoEMetricSpace route rather than introducing a separate graph-ball API up front.

Side note: this community feels welcoming. As a new contributor I really appreciate that.

Oh one downside of PseudoEMetricSpace is that it requires importing the reals, which is unfortunate.
So maybe we should have graph-specific balls, I guess it depends on what you plan to use them for, since existing graph-theory files wouldn't be able to import these.

The use case I have in mind is discrete graph metric arguments with nat or ℕ∞ radii, especially basic lemmas about balls and spheres, monotonicity, connected-component behavior at radius ⊤, and eventually cardinality bounds in terms of degree and radius. If going through PseudoEMetricSpace pulls in Real machinery that we do not actually use, then a small graph-specific API may be the better first step.
Then perhaps we should just have SimpleGraph.eball? And since balls with dist (and not edist) don't make a lot of sense in non-connected graphs, we can drop the e?

That seems reasonable to me. If the intended use is graph-metric arguments inside SimpleGraph rather than a more general PseudoEMetricSpace interface, then SimpleGraph.ball with a small first-pass API sounds like the right direction. If this is agreeable to y'all, I can draft the PR for review.
Good morning y'all, the PR draft is nearly ready, expect it to land on the mathlib repo in the next 1-2 hours. Thank you for your guidance.
All done, I welcome any feedback you may have: https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/36443

Hello @Laura Monk and @Snir Broshi - I’m touching base about PR #36443.

I noticed the LLM-Generated label was added and there hasn’t been any recent activity. I’m happy to revise the PR further if needed; if the current blocker is scope, naming, or just reviewer bandwidth, a quick pointer would help me steer it in the right direction.

I'm sure there’s an active discussion around AI-assisted contributions and review load. I don’t want to derail the PR thread, but I do want to be useful here long-term. If there’s a better thread for that discussion, I’d be glad to join it. I’m especially interested in what concrete practices would make AI-assisted PRs easier for maintainers to trust and review.
If you are a new contributor it is better if you do not use AI in your first few PRs since it helps you learn lean better and understand what reviewers are looking for.

Nelson Spence said:

if the current blocker is scope, naming, or just reviewer bandwidth

The blocker is indeed reviewer bandwidth, see the queueboard for a list of PRs waiting to be reviewed

Nelson Spence said:

If there’s a better thread for that discussion, I’d be glad to join it.

#mathlib4 > What to do with "slop" PRs
#mathlib4 > policy proposal: mention AI use in PR description?

Other large threads about formalizing using LLMs but not for Mathlib

#Machine Learning for Theorem Proving > Discussion: AI-written mathematical proofs
#Machine Learning for Theorem Proving > Are human mathematicians becoming redundant?
#general > sloplib
#general > The role of AI companies in large formalisation projects

Nelson Spence said:

I’m especially interested in what concrete practices would make AI-assisted PRs easier for maintainers to trust and review.

AFAIK they are trusted iff the human supervising them is a known and trusted Lean expert that has read the entire output, which goes back to what Shreyas recommended

Thank you @Snir Broshi and @Shreyas Srinivas for the replies. I can see that the concern here is reviewer trust and reviewer time, and that handwritten early PRs feel like a simpler signal from your side.

I’ll take the broader discussion to the policy threads you linked above.

Thank you as well for answering directly about the blocker on this PR. I really appreciate the way you all have guided me through my first contribution experience. :thank_you:
